head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proof is the same as in \cite[Theorem 4.4]{BV}, except that instead of taking $P\rightarrow S$ a $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibration in the definition of the various stacks, we take $P=\mathbb{P} V\rightarrow S$ where $V$ is a rank $2$ vector bundle with trivial determinant.
head: environment

label: exc1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exc1}
Let $T_{\pi} = \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{P}}(2)$ denote the relative tangent bundle of $\pi: \mathcal{P} \to \mathcal{V}_{r,d}$, so the the relative Todd class is $\mathrm{Td} _{\pi} = 1 + \frac{1}{2} c_1(T_{\pi}) + \ldots = 1 + z + \ldots$. Using Equation \eqref{idT}, and then Grothedieck--Riemann--Roch, we have that on $\mathcal{V}_{r,d}$,
\begin{align*} 
t_1 &= c_1(\pi_*\mathcal{E}(-1)) = \operatorname{ch}_1(\pi_*\mathcal{E}(-1)) = [\pi_*(\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{E}) \cdot \operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{P}}(-1))\cdot \mathrm{Td}_{\pi})]_1 \\
&= [\pi_*(\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{E}) \cdot (1 - z) \cdot (1 + z))]_1 = \pi_*(\operatorname{ch}_2(\mathcal{E})) = \pi_*\left(\frac{1}{2}c_1(\mathcal{E})^2 - c_2(\mathcal{E})\right) \\
&= da_1 - a_2' \\
u_1 &= c_1(\pi_*\mathcal{E}) = \operatorname{ch}_1(\pi_*\mathcal{E}) = [\pi_*(\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{E}) \cdot \mathrm{Td}_{\pi})]_1 = [\pi_*(\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{E}) \cdot (1 + z))]_1 \\
&= \pi_*(\operatorname{ch}_2(\mathcal{E}) +  \operatorname{ch}_1(\mathcal{E})z) = (da_1 - a_2') + a_1 \\
&= (d+1)a_1 - a_2'.
\end{align*}
It follows that $a_1 = u_1 - t_1$ and $a_2' =du_1 - (d+1)t_1$.

label: int-pic
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: leftes
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B}G)$ is naturally identified with the character group of $G$ because it is identified with Mumford's functorial Picard group.                 
The exact sequence of groups
\[0 \rightarrow \mu_2 \rightarrow G_{r,d,s,e} \times \operatorname{SL}_2 \rightarrow \Gamma_{r,d,s,e} \rightarrow 0\]
induces a left exact sequence
\begin{equation} \label{leftes}0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B}\Gamma_{r,d,s,e}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B}( G_{r,d,s,e} \times \operatorname{SL}_2)) \rightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B}\mu_2).
\end{equation}
The Picard group  $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B}\mu_2)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Let $h$ be a generator of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B} \mu_2)$.
Recall that the map $\mu_2 \to G_{r,d,s,e} \times \operatorname{SL}_2$ sends $-1$ to $(-\operatorname{Id}_d, \operatorname{Id}_{r+d}, -\operatorname{Id}_e, \operatorname{Id}_{s+e}, -\operatorname{Id}_2)$. 
The generator $t_1 \in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathrm{B}(G_{r,d,s,e} \times \operatorname{SL}_2))$ corresponds to the determinant of the rank $d$ matrix. Thus, the right-hand map in \eqref{leftes} sends $t_1$ to $dh$. Similarly,
$u_1$ and $w_1$ are sent to zero, and $v_1$ to $eh$. The kernel is thus the subgroup generated by the classes listed in \eqref{gens1}.

The translation between \eqref{gens1} and \eqref{gens2} follows from Example \ref{exc1}. We explain the case $d, e$ both odd, the other cases being similar but simpler. Since $d$ and $e$ are both odd, the following change of basis matrix has integer coefficients
\[\left(\begin{matrix} t_1 - v_1 \\ 2t_1 \\ u_1 \\ w_1 \end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix} e & \frac{d - e}{2} & -1 & 1 \\[3pt]
0 & d & -2 & 0 \\[3pt]
0 & \frac{d+1}{2} & -1 & 0 \\[3pt]
-(e+1) & \frac{e+1}{2} & 0 & -1
\end{matrix} \right)\left(\begin{matrix} a_1 - b_1 \\ 2a_1 \\ a_2' \\ b_2' \end{matrix}\right). \]
The determinant of the $4 \times 4$ matrix above is $1$ so the entries of the two column vectors generate the same subgroup with $\mathbb{Z}$-coefficients.

label: gm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{gm}
Suppose that $X\rightarrow Y$ is a $\mathbb{G}_m$-torsor with associated line bundle $\mathcal{L}$. Then,
\[
\operatorname{Pic}(X)\cong \operatorname{Pic}(Y)/\langle c_1(\mathcal{L})\rangle.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Under the correspondence between $\mathbb{G}_m$-torsors and line bundles, $X$ is the complement of the zero section in the total space of the line bundle $\mathcal{L}\rightarrow Y$. We thus have the exact sequence
\[
\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\rightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{L})\rightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(X)\rightarrow 0.
\]
After identifying $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{L})$ with $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$, the first map in the sequence is given by multiplication by the first Chern class $c_1(\mathcal{L})$, and the result follows.
head: environment

label: hack
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{hack}
Let $\mathscr{P}^k \to \mathscr{M}_2$ be as above. Then the pullback map $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{P}^k)$ is injective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There are natural isomorphisms $\mathscr{P}^k \cong \mathscr{P}^{k+2}$ (given by tensoring with the canonical), so it suffices to prove the claim for $k = 2$ and $k = 3$. When $k = 2$, the canonical line bundle gives a section $\mathscr{M}_2 \to \mathscr{P}^k$, so the pullback map must be injective. 

Now consider the case $k = 3$. Every degree $3$ line bundle on a genus $2$ curve has $2$ sections. Therefore, $\mathscr{H}_{3,2}$ is naturally an open substack inside $\mathscr{P}^3$. (It is the complement of the universal curve $\mathscr{C} \hookrightarrow \mathscr{P}^3$ embedded by summing each point with a canonical divisor.) The isomorphism $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,2})$ factors through $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{P}^3)$, so the latter must also be injective.
head: environment

label: cb
title: Proof
body_md:
Using excision, for $g \geq 3$, we have
\[\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,g}^s) = \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,g})/\langle T \rangle = \frac{\mathbb{Z}(\epsilon a_1) \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2'}{\langle \left(\frac{8g+12}{\epsilon}\right)\epsilon a_1 - 9a_2', \left(\frac{24g+36}{\epsilon}\right) \epsilon a_1 - 24a_2'\rangle}\]
Now observe that
\begin{equation} \label{cb}
\left(\begin{matrix} -8 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 \end{matrix}\right) \left(\begin{matrix} (8g+12)/\epsilon & -9 \\ (24g+36)/\epsilon & -24 \end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix} (8g + 12)/\epsilon & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{matrix} \right).
\end{equation}
The matrix on the left of \eqref{cb} is invertible over $\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,g}^s)$ is the sum of two cyclic groups with orders given by the diagonal entries of the matrix on the right of \eqref{cb}.
This completes the proof for $g \geq 3$.

Finally, for $g = 2$, we already know $a_2'= 2a_1$ by \eqref{s13} and that $10a_1 = 0$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,g})$. When we remove $T$, this creates one additional relation $0 = T = 84a_1-24a_2' = 36a_1$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,g}^s)$. We have $\gcd(10,36) = 2$, so $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{3,2}^s) = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
head: environment

label: k4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{k4}
If $g \neq 3$, every component of the complement of $\mathscr{H}'_{4,g}\subset \mathscr{H}_{4,g}$ has codimension at least $2$. Hence, there is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}) \cong \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}')$.
head: environment

label: cc4
title: Proof
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Each $M(E, F)$ can be constructed directly as a global quotient, giving rise to a bound on $\operatorname{Pic}(M(E, F))$.
Deopurkar--Patel use their enumeration of the components of $\mathcal{H}_{4,g} \smallsetminus M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_{\operatorname{gen}})$ to count ranks and prove the Picard rank conjecture for $k \leq 5$. 

The new innovation in our work is that we have built a larger open $\mathscr{H}_{4,g}'$ which contains several $M(E, F)$
and, in particular, is not missing any divisorial components (when $g \neq 3$). Hence, we see $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}) = \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}')$, and we can compute the later \emph{integrally} using excision on $\mathscr{H}_{4,g}' \subset \mathscr{X}_{4,g}'$.
head: environment

label: g3lem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{g3lem}
When $g = 3$, the complement of $\mathscr{H}_{4,3}' \subset \mathscr{H}_{4,3}$ is an irreducible divisor whose class lies in the subgroup generated by $\epsilon a_1$ and $a_2'$ (these classes are defined on all of $\mathscr{H}_{4,3}$ via pull back along $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}_{4,3}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g})$.)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Continuing the notation of the previous lemma, first note that if \[M(\mathcal{O}(1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(2) \oplus \mathcal{O}(3), \mathcal{O}(f_1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(f_2)) \neq \varnothing\]
then by \cite[Proposition 5.6(2)]{part1}, we have $f_1 \leq 2$ and $f_2 \leq 4$ and $f_1 + f_2 = 6$, hence $f_1 = 2$ and $f_2 = 4$.
The divisor in \eqref{weird3} can therefore be viewed as the locus were the universal $\mathscr{E}$ (pulled back along $\mathscr{H}_{4,3} \to \mathscr{B}_{4,3}$) has splitting type $(1, 2, 3)$ on fibers of the universal $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibration. 
 As a splitting locus for $\mathscr{E}$, this divisor occurs in the expected codimension, so its fundamental class is determined by the universal splitting loci formulas of \cite{L}. In particular, it can be expressed in terms of the classes $\epsilon a_1, a_2'$.
head: environment

label: allc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{allc}
For $g \geq 2$, some combination of components of $\mathscr{D}_{4,g}$ has class
\[\frac{8g+20}{\epsilon}(\epsilon a_1) - 8a_2' - b_2' \in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}'_{4,g}) \cong \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}_{4,g}'). \]
In particular, an integral relation holds in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}')$ expressing $b_2'$ in terms of $\epsilon a_1$ and $a_2'$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Base changing \eqref{scr4} by $\operatorname{BSL}_2 \to \operatorname{BPGL}_2$, we obtain the stacks and morphisms considered in \cite[Section 5.2]{part1} (below $\Delta_{4,g}'$ is the complement of the open inclusion $\mathcal{H}_{4,g}' \hookrightarrow \mathcal{X}_{4,g}'$ of \cite[Lemma 5.3]{part1}):
\[\Delta_{4,g}' \to \mathcal{X}_{4,g}' \rightarrow \mathcal{B}_{4,g}' \rightarrow \mathcal{B}_{4,g} \rightarrow \mathcal{V}_{3,g+3} \times_{\operatorname{BSL}_2} \mathcal{V}_{2,g+3} \rightarrow \operatorname{BSL}_2. \]
We claim some combination of components of $\Delta_{4,g}'$ has class
\[(8g + 20)a_1 - 8a_2' - b_2'\in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{X}'_{4,g}) \cong \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{B}_{4,g}). \]
 This will establish the lemma since the map $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}'_{4,g}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{X}'_{4,g})$
 sends the class of a component of $\mathscr{D}_{4,g}$ to the class of the corresponding component of $\Delta_{4,g}'$. Because $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}'_{4,g}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{X}'_{4,g})$  is injective (by Lemma \ref{comparison}), classes are represented by the same formulas in either group.

By \cite[Lemma 5.2 and Equation 5.7]{part2}, we know that $(8g + 20)a_1 - 8a_2' - b_2' = 0$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{H}_{4,g})$, so this relation must also hold on the open substack $\mathcal{H}_{4,g}' \subset \mathcal{H}_{4,g}$. But, we also know $\mathcal{H}_{4,g}' \cong \mathcal{X}'_{4,g} \smallsetminus \Delta_{4,g}'$. By excision, every relation among $a_1, a_2', b_2'$ restricted to $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{H}_{4,g}')$ comes from a class supported on $\Delta_{4,g}' \subset \mathcal{X}'_{4,g}$. That is, some combination of components of $\Delta_{4,g}'$ has class $(8g + 20)a_1 - 8a_2' - b_2' = 0$. The corresponding
combination of components of $\mathscr{D}_{4,g}$ will have the same class.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In fact, the fundamental class of $\mathscr{D}_{4,g}$ 
has the class displayed in Lemma \ref{allc}.
For a more conceptual explanation, we sketch the following argument.
Recall that in \cite[Equation 5.7]{part2}, we computed the restriction of $[\Delta_{4,g}']$ to a slightly smaller open $\mathcal{X}_{4,g}^\circ \subset \mathcal{X}'_{4,g}$ via principal parts bundle techniques. For $g$ sufficiently large, the complement of $\mathcal{X}_{4,g}^\circ \subset \mathcal{X}'_{4,g}$ has codimension at least $2$, so the codimesnion $1$ calculation holds on all of $\mathcal{X}'_{4,g}$.
That is $[\Delta_{4,g}'] = (8g+20)a_1 - 8a_2' - b_2'$ and so $[\mathscr{D}_{4,g}]$ also has this class.

But even for smaller $g$, 
we claim the formula for $[\Delta_{4,g}]$ in \cite[Equation 5.7]{part2} holds on all of $\mathcal{X}_{4,g}'$. Although the principal parts map of \cite[Equation 5.4]{part2} need not be surjective over all of $\mathcal{X}_{4,g}'$ (so the vanishing locus $\widetilde{\Delta}_{4,g}$ of the principal parts bundle map need not be a vector bundle) 
the calculation of the fundamental class holds so long as $\widetilde{\Delta}_{4,g}$ has the correct codimension. One can verify this by stratifying the base by loci where the rank drops and checking that the strata where the rank drops by $\delta$ have codimension greater than $\delta$. This also establishes irreducibility of $\Delta_{4,g}'$ and $\mathscr{D}_{4,g}$ when $g \geq 4$. However, this fact is not actually necessary for our argument.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By excision, we know that
\[\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}') \cong \frac{\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}_{4,g}')}{\text{classes supported on $\mathscr{D}_{4,g}$}}.\]
Meanwhile, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}_{4,g}')$ is a quotient of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}_{4,g}) =\mathbb{Z} (\epsilon a_1) \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2' \oplus \mathbb{Z} b_2'$ (see \eqref{pb4}).
Hence, using Lemma \ref{allc}, we see $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}')$ is a quotient of
\[\frac{\mathbb{Z} (\epsilon a_1) \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2' \oplus \mathbb{Z} b_2'}{\langle \frac{8g+20}{\epsilon}(\epsilon a_1) - 8a_2' - b_2' \rangle} \cong \mathbb{Z} (\epsilon a_1) \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2'. \]


Recall that in Lemma \ref{k4}, we showed $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}) = \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}')$ for $g \geq 4$. By \cite[Proposition 2.15]{DP}, this group has rank at least $2$. Therefore, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}) = \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}$, since any quotient would have smaller rank.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{g3lem}, the  kernel of the restriction map \[
\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3}')\]
lies in the subgroup $\langle a_1, a_2' \rangle$. We know that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}'_{4,g})$ is generated by the classes $a_1, a_2', b_2'$, so it follows that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3})$ is also generated by these $3$ classes.

Next, we claim that $b_2'$ is integrally expressible in terms of $a_1, a_2'$.
By Lemma \ref{allc}, we know $b_2'$ is expressible in terms of $a_1, a_2'$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3}')$.
But, the kernel of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3}')$ lies in $\langle a_1, a_2' \rangle$, so $b_2'$ must also be expressible in terms of $a_1, a_2'$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3})$.

It follows that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3})$ is a quotient of $\mathbb{Z} a_1 \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2'$.
However, by \cite{DP}, we know that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,3})$ has rank $2$. Any further quotient would have lower rank, so we are done.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have already established that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ is generated by $2a_1$ and $a_2'$.  Using Example \ref{exc1}, we compute that (see \eqref{univdiagram} for definitions of the maps $f, \alpha, \pi$)
\[\lambda = c_1(f_*\omega_f) = c_1(\pi_*(\alpha_* \omega_\alpha) \otimes \omega_\pi) = c_1(\pi_*\mathcal{E}(-2)) = 4a_1 - a_2' = 2(2 a_1) - a_2'.\]
From this we see that $\lambda$ and $2a_1$ are generators for $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$. Since $\lambda$ is the generator of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/10\mathbb{Z}$, we see that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ is a quotient of $\mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/10$. 

By the discussion at the start of this section, we know $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ has rank at least $1$.
Thus, it remains to prove that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ is injective.

Let $\mathscr{P}^k$ be the universal Picard variety over $\mathscr{M}_2$ as in Section \ref{gb3} (the $\mathbb{G}_m$-rigidification of the universal Picard stack $\mathscr{P}ic^k$).
As in \cite[Section 6]{Mochizuki}, the natural map $\mathscr{H}_{4,2} \to \mathscr{P}^4$ factors through a Grassmann fibration. For this, recall that every degree $4$ line bundle on a genus $2$ curve has a $3$-dimensional space of sections.
Let $\mathscr{G} \to \mathscr{P}^4$ be the Grassmann fibration 
parametrizing two-dimensional subspaces of the space of global sections of a degree $4$ line bundle. Then 
$\mathscr{H}_{4,2}$ sits naturally as an open substack $\mathscr{G}$.
                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
Its complement $Z = \mathscr{G} \smallsetminus \mathscr{H}_{4,2}$ is the locus of pencils with a base point. Note that $Z$ has $1$-dimensional irreducible fibers over $\mathscr{P}^4$, so $Z$ is irreducible. Since $Z$ meets each fiber of $\mathscr{G} \to  \mathscr{P}^4$, it is not equivalent to the pullback of a divisor on $\mathscr{P}^4$. In particular, the map $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{P}^4) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ must be injective. Using Lemma \ref{hack}, we conclude that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ is also injective, completing the proof.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Geometrically, the fact that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,2})$ has rank $1$ can be explained by the fact that $\Delta_{4,2}'$ is reducible. Thus, its components give rise to further relations beyond just its fundamental class.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By excision, we have $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g}^s) = \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{4,g})/\langle T, D \rangle$.
 Row operations over $\mathbb{Z}$ diagonalize the change of basis matrix for $\epsilon a_1, a_2'$ to $T, D$, namely we have
\[\left(\begin{matrix} 3 & 2 \\
4&3\end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} (24g+60)/\epsilon & -24 \\
(-32g-80)/\epsilon & 36\end{matrix}\right) = 
\left(\begin{matrix} (8g+20)/\epsilon & 0 \\
0 & 12\end{matrix}\right),
\]
where the matrix on the left is invertible over $\mathbb{Z}$.
By its definition in \eqref{epsilondef}, we have $\epsilon = 1$ when $g$ is odd and $\epsilon = 2$ when $g$ is even, so
the corollary follows for $g \geq 3$. 

Finally, when $g = 2$, the above tells us $18(2a_1) = 0$ and $12a_2' = 0$, and we have the additional relation 
\[0 = 10\lambda = 10(4a_1 - a_2') \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad 0 = 2(2a_1 + a_2').\]
Using generators $2a_1 + a_2'$ and $2a_1$, we see that they generate cyclic groups of order $2$ and $18$ respectively.
head: environment

label: c5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{c5}
Suppose $g \neq 3$. Then, every component of the complement of $\mathscr{H}'_{5,g}\subset \mathscr{H}_{5,g}$ has codimension at least $2$. In particular, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g}) = \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g}')$
head: environment

label: cc
title: Proof
body_md:
Following the notation of \cite{DP},
let $M(E, F) \subset \mathscr{H}_{5,g}$ denote the locus of covers $\alpha$ with $E_\alpha \cong E$ and $F_\alpha \cong F$. 
The complement of $\mathscr{H}'_{5,g}\subset \mathscr{H}_{5,g}$ is the union of $M(E, F)$ such that
\begin{equation} \label{cc}
h^1(E \otimes \det E^\vee \otimes \wedge^2 F^\vee) > 0.
\end{equation}
If $E = \mathcal{O}(e_1) \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathcal{O}(e_4)$ with $e_1 \leq \cdots \leq e_4$ and $F = \mathcal{O}(f_1) \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathcal{O}(f_5)$ with $f_1 \leq \cdots \leq f_5$, then \eqref{cc} is equivalent to $e_1 + f_1 + f_2 - (g+4) \leq -2$.

Next, let
$E_{\operatorname{gen}}$, respectively $F_{\operatorname{gen}}$, denote the balanced bundle of rank $4$ and degree $g+4$, respectively rank $5$ and degree $2g+8$.
First note that $h^1(E_{\operatorname{gen}} \otimes \det E_{\operatorname{gen}}^\vee \otimes \wedge^2 F_{\operatorname{gen}}^\vee) = 0$, as in this case, $e_1 + f_1 + f_2 - (g+4) \geq \lfloor \frac{g+4}{4} \rfloor + 2 \lfloor \frac{2(g+4)}{5} \rfloor - (g+4) \geq -1$ (except when $g = 3$, in which case $f_2 = \lceil \frac{2(g+4)}{5}\rceil$, so we still have $e_1 + f_1+f_2 \geq -1$.)
This says that $M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_{\operatorname{gen}}) \subseteq \mathscr{H}_{5,g}'$. Hence, any divisorial component of $\mathscr{H}_{5,g} \smallsetminus \mathscr{H}_{5,g}'$ is contained in a divisorial component of $\mathscr{H}_{5,g} \smallsetminus M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_{\operatorname{gen}})$.

Again, let us define bundles that are ``one-off" from balanced
\begin{align*}
    F_1 &:= \mathcal{O}(n-1) \oplus \oplus \mathcal{O}(n)^{\oplus 3} \mathcal{O}(n+1) & \qquad & \text{if $n = \frac{2g+8}{5}$ is an integer} \\
    E_1 &:= \mathcal{O}(m-1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(m)^{\oplus 2} \oplus \mathcal{O}(m+1) & \qquad &\text{if $m = \frac{g+4}{4}$ is an integer.}
\end{align*}
In \cite[p. 25]{DP}, Deopurkar--Patel enumerate the divisorial components of $\mathscr{H}_{5,g} \smallsetminus M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_{\operatorname{gen}})$ and show that, for $g \neq 3$, they are always of the form \begin{align*}
    &\overline{M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_1)} &\qquad &\text{if $5 \mid 2g+8$} \\
    &\overline{M(E_1, F_{\operatorname{gen}})} &\qquad &\text{if $4 \mid g+4$}.
\end{align*}
Note that we are using the irreducibility of $M$ and $CE$ in \cite[Propositions 5.1 and 5.2]{DP} to write these divisors as the closures above.
One readily checks that
\[h^1(E_{\operatorname{gen}} \otimes \det E^\vee_{\operatorname{gen}} \otimes \wedge^2 F_1) = h^1(E_1 \otimes \det E_1^\vee \otimes \wedge^2 F_{\operatorname{gen}}) = 0\]
Hence, when they are defined, $\mathscr{H}_{5,g}'$ contains each of 
\[M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_{\operatorname{gen}}), \quad M(E_{\operatorname{gen}}, F_1), \quad M(E_1, F_{\operatorname{gen}}),\]
and all other possible $M(E, F)$ have codimension at least $2$.
head: environment

label: g3prime
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{g3prime}
When $g=3$, the complement of $\mathscr{H}'_{5,3}\subset \mathscr{H}_{5,3}$ is an irreducible divisor whose class lies in the subgroup generated by $2 a_1$ and $a_2'$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The divisorial component of the complement of $\mathscr{H}_{5,3}'$ inside $\mathscr{H}_{5,3}$ is the locus
\[
\overline{M(E_1, F_1)} = \overline{M(\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(2)^{\oplus 3},\mathcal{O}(2)^{\oplus 2}\oplus \mathcal{O}(3)^{\oplus 2}\oplus \mathcal{O}(4))}.
\]
By \cite[Proposition 5.2]{DP}, this locus is precisely the preimage of the hyperelliptic locus under the natural morphism $\mathscr{H}_{5,3}\rightarrow \mathscr{M}_3$. By \cite{DL}, the hyperelliptic locus in $\mathscr{M}_3$ has class $9\lambda$. 
The class $\lambda = c_1(f_*\omega_f) = c_1(\pi_* \mathscr{E} \otimes \omega_{\pi}) \in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3})$ is pulled back from $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}_{5,3})$. Since $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}_{5,3})$ includes into $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{B}_{5,3})$, we can determine this class via a calculation on the $\operatorname{SL}_2$ quotient, as in Example \ref{exc1}:
\[
[\overline{M(E_1, F_1)}] = 9\lambda=9c_1(f_*\omega_f)=9c_1(\pi_*\mathcal{E}(-2))=54a_1-9a_2' = 27(2 a_1) - 9a_2',
\]
which is in the span of $2a_1$ and $a_2'$.

label: d5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{d5}
For $g\geq 2$, some combination of the components of $\mathscr{D}_{5,g}$ has class
\[
\frac{(10g+36)}{\epsilon}(\epsilon a_1)-7a_2'-b_2'\in \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}'_{5,g})\cong \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}'_{5,g}).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Base changing \eqref{scr5} by $\operatorname{BSL}_2 \to \operatorname{BPGL}_2$, we obtain the stacks and morphisms considered in \cite[Section 5.3]{part1} (below $\Delta_{5,g}'$ is the complement of the open inclusion $\mathcal{H}_{5,g}' \hookrightarrow \mathcal{X}_{5,g}'$ of \cite[Lemma 5.11]{part1}):
\[\Delta_{5,g}' \to \mathcal{X}_{5,g}' \rightarrow \mathcal{B}_{5,g}' \rightarrow \mathcal{B}_{5,g} \rightarrow \mathcal{V}_{4,g+4} \times_{\operatorname{BSL}_2} \mathcal{V}_{5,2g+8} \rightarrow \operatorname{BSL}_2. \]
By \cite[Lemma 6.6 and Equation 6.19]{part2}, the relation $\frac{(10g+36)}{\epsilon}(\epsilon a_1)-7a_2'-b_2'=0$ holds in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal{H}_{5,g})$, so it must also hold on the open substack $\mathcal{H}'_{5,g}$. Since $\mathcal{H}'_{5,g}=\mathcal{X}'_{5,g}\smallsetminus \Delta_{5,g}'$, any relation among $a_1, a_2', b_2'$ on $\mathcal{H}'_{5,g}$ must come from a class supported on $\Delta_{5,g}'$. Therefore, some combination of components of $\Delta_{5,g}'$ has class $(10g+36)a_1-7a_2'-b_2'$. The corresponding combination of components on $\mathscr{D}_{5,g}$ has the same class.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{c5}, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g})\cong \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g}')$ for $g\geq 4$. We have that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}'_{5,g})$ is a quotient of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{X}'_{5,g})\cong \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{B}'_{5,g})$ by classes supported on $\mathscr{D}_{5,g}$. By Lemma \ref{d5}, one such class is $(10g+36)a_1-7a_2'-b_2'$. Therefore, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}'_{5,g})$ is a quotient of 
\[
\frac{\mathbb{Z} (\epsilon a_1) \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2' \oplus \mathbb{Z} b_2'}{\langle \frac{10g+36}{\epsilon}(\epsilon a_1) - 7a_2' - b_2' \rangle} \cong \mathbb{Z} (\epsilon a_1) \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2'.
\]
By \cite[Proposition 2.15]{DP}, the rank of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g})\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is at least $2$, so we must have that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g})\cong \mathbb{Z}(\epsilon a_1)\oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2'$.

name: Proof of Theorem 1.1(3) when $g\geq 4$

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{g3prime}, the  kernel of the restriction map \[\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3}')\] lies in the subgroup $\langle 2a_1, a_2' \rangle$. We know that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}'_{5,g})$ is generated by the classes $a_1, a_2', b_2'$, so it follows that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3})$ is also generated by these $3$ classes.

Next, we claim that $b_2'$ is integrally expressible in terms of $a_1, a_2'$.
By Lemma \ref{d5}, we know $b_2'$ is expressible in terms of $a_1, a_2'$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3}')$.
But, the kernel of $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3}) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3}')$ lies in $\langle a_1, a_2' \rangle$, so $b_2'$ must also be expressible in terms of $a_1, a_2'$ in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3})$.

It follows that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3})$ is a quotient of $\mathbb{Z} a_1 \oplus \mathbb{Z} a_2'$.
However, by \cite{DP}, we know that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3})\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ has rank $2$, so $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,3})\cong \mathbb{Z}\oplus \mathbb{Z}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We have already established that $a_1, a_2'$ are generators for $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,2})$. We compute directly $\lambda = 5a_1 - a_2'$ as in Section \ref{4genus2}, from which we see $\lambda$ and $a_1$ are generators for  $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,2})$.
Arguing as in Section \ref{4genus2}, it suffices to show that the map $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,2})$ is injective.


Every degree $5$ line bundle on a genus $2$ curve has a $4$-dimensional space of sections. The Hurwitz space $\mathscr{H}_{5,2}$ then sits naturally as an open inside the Grassmann fibration $\mathscr{G} \to \mathscr{P}^5$ parametrizing $2$-dimensional subspaces of the space of global sections of a degree $5$ line bundle.
The complement of $\mathscr{H}_{5,2} \subset \mathscr{G}$ is the locus of pencils with a base point, which we again see is irreducible and not equivalent to the pullback of a divisor on $\mathscr{P}^5$. In particular, the map $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{P}^5) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,2})$ must be injective. Applying Lemma \ref{hack}, we conclude that $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{M}_2) \to \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,2})$ is also injective, completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
By excision $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g}^s) = \operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g})/\langle T, D \rangle$.
 Again, row operations over $\mathbb{Z}$ diagonalize the change of basis matrix for $\epsilon a_1, a_2'$ to $T, D$:
\[\left(\begin{matrix} 3 & 2 \\
4&3\end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} (24g+84)/\epsilon & -24 \\
(-32g-112)/\epsilon & 36\end{matrix}\right) = 
\left(\begin{matrix} (8g+28)/\epsilon & 0 \\
0 & 12\end{matrix}\right).
\]
For $g \geq 3$, these are the only relations, so $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathscr{H}_{5,g}^s)$ is the sum of two cyclic groups of orders equal to the diagonal entries above.

In genus $2$, the above gives $44a_1 = 0$ and $12a_2' =0$, and we have the additional relation 
\[0 = 10\lambda = 10(5a_1 - a_2') \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad 0 = 2(3a_1 + a_2')\]
The generators $a_1$ and $3a_1+a_2'$ generate cyclic groups of order $44$ and $2$ respectively.
